extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, students, and teachers of English (users seeking grammar/style guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and descriptive rules for correct English grammar and usage, covering modifiers, verb properties (voice, mood, tense, person, number), auxiliaries, be-verbs, and adverb formation/placement. Aimed to guide sentence-level correctness and stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangling participles (danglers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A participial phrase must attach to a logical subject; otherwise it produces a dangling modifier with no clear subject (a 'dangler').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct by supplying a logical subject or using active voice so the participle precedes the noun it modifies. Example: change a passive dangler to active voice: 'finding that the questions were not ambiguous, the teacher did not change the exam grades.' Avoid constructions like 'Reviewing the suggestions, it is clear that no consensus exists.' (Better: 'Our review of the suggestions shows that no consensus exists.') See also cross-references (e.g., 5.116, 5.175).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangling gerunds
rubrics_metrics.description: A gerund functioning as the object of a preposition may be misinterpreted as a modifier and leave the actor unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise the sentence to clarify the subject of the gerund. Example poor: 'After finishing the research, the screenplay was easy to write.' Better: 'After Gero finished the research, the screenplay was easy to write' or 'After finishing the research, Gero found the screenplay easy to write.' Beware improbable readings (e.g., 'While driving to San Antonio, my phone ran out of power' — clarify to 'While I was driving ...'). Compare related rules (5.115).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb properties (voice, mood, tense, person, number)
rubrics_metrics.description: A verb has five properties—voice, mood, tense, person, and number—and is conjugated to show them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these five properties is foundational to correct verb usage and agreement; subsequent sections address each property in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active and passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice indicates whether the subject performs (active) or receives (passive) the action. Only transitive verbs have voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive is formed by an inflected form of 'to be' (or colloquially 'get') + past participle. As a matter of style, passive voice is typically, though not always, inferior to active voice; choose based on the desired point of view (e.g., mouse was caught by the cat vs the cat caught the mouse). Be able to identify passive voice reliably; the mere presence of a be-verb does not always indicate passive (e.g., 'he is thinking' is not passive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive conjugation and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive conjugation is formed by an inflected form of 'be' + a verb's present participle; whether it's active or passive depends on the verb and auxiliaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inflected 'be' joins a present participle (the ox is pulling the cart), the progressive is active for transitive verbs. If both the principal and auxiliary are be-verbs followed by a past participle (the cart is being pulled), the result is passive voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicative mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The indicative mood expresses facts, opinions, and asks questions—the most common mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'amethysts cost very little', 'the botanist lives in a garden cottage', 'does that bush produce yellow roses?'. Use indicative for statements that are (or may be) true rather than imagined or conditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperative mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperative expresses commands, direct requests, and sometimes permission; subject 'you' is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formed by the verb stem (e.g., 'go away!', 'bring the tray in here'). Use cautiously—imperatives can be blunt or rude; soften with 'please' or recast into the indicative (e.g., 'will you stop at the store, please?'). Direct addresses are not the subject (e.g., 'Cindy, take good care of yourself').

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjunctive mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjunctive expresses actions or states as doubtful, imagined, desired, conditional, hypothetical, or contrary to fact; less frequent in modern English but still useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persists in stock expressions ('perish the thought', 'heaven help us', 'be that as it may') and signals non-reality: wishes, conjectures, demands, suggestions. See examples in following entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjunctive versus indicative (common errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish when the subjunctive is required versus when the indicative is appropriate; three common errors are identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors: (1) Using indicative when subjunctive is needed (Poor: 'If it wasn't for your help...' Better: 'If it weren't for your help...'). (2) Treating sentences that resemble subjunctive constructions but are factual (Poor: 'I called to see whether she were in.' Better: 'I called to see whether she was in.'). (3) Incorrect double conditional 'If I would have gone...' instead of 'If I had gone...'. Note: not every 'if' clause takes subjunctive; use indicative when the action might be true but unknown (e.g., 'If I am right about this, please call').

rubrics_metrics.name: Present subjunctive mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Formed by using the base form of the verb (e.g., 'be') and appears in suggestions or requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'he recommended that we be ready at a moment's notice', 'we insist that he retain control of the accounting department'. The present subjunctive can also be expressed using 'be' plus simple-past form or a past-form auxiliary + infinitive in some constructions (examples provided). See also related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past subjunctive mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The past-tense subjunctive typically refers to something present or future but contrary to fact; formed with the simple-past tense, except 'be' becomes 'were' regardless of number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'If I were king', 'If she were any different'. Past subjunctive uses past-tense morphology to connote uncertainty or unreality in present/future contexts (compare indicative forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Past-perfect subjunctive mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses the past-perfect form (had + past participle) to refer to past situations contrary to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'If he had been there', 'If I had gone'. The past-perfect subjunctive signals hypothetical past alternatives (compare indicative: 'If it arrived, it was not properly filed' vs subjunctive: 'If it had arrived, it could have changed the course of history').

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb tense (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tense shows the time of an act/state/condition; main divisions are present, past, future, each with perfect forms and optional progressive forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are six basic tenses (present, past, future, present perfect, past perfect, future perfect), and each can be progressive. Understand distinctions between tenses for correct temporal reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present tense
rubrics_metrics.description: The present tense (infinitive stem) denotes present acts, conditions, habitual actions, timeless facts, and is used for the historical present in fiction/analysis of literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses: (1) present actions ('the dog howls'), (2) habitual/general truths ('cats prowl nightly'), (3) refer to timeless facts or enduring works ('Julius Caesar describes...'), (4) narrate fictional plots (historical-present). Use present-perfect to distinguish present action vs past when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past indicative tense (formation and irregulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotes actions occurring at an explicit or implicit past time; regular verbs add -ed with spelling rules; irregular verbs vary (e.g., give-gave-given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spelling notes: verbs ending in -e add -d; verbs ending -y preceded by consonant change y to i; doubling final consonants under certain stress/syllable conditions (differences noted for British English). Use a good reference for irregulars; see cross-references (5.100).

rubrics_metrics.name: Future tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally formed with 'will' + verb stem; refers to expected future acts or conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Shall' may be used in first-person questions or legal statements; many linguists treat English as having no technical future tense (will is a modal), but traditional usage treats will as future. For legal requirements, 'shall' or 'must' may be preferred ('the debtor shall pay within 30 days').

rubrics_metrics.name: Present-perfect tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Formed with have/has + past participle; denotes actions completed or continuing up to the present or indefinite past touching the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from simple past by indicating an indefinite past or action that reaches into the present ('I have put away the clothes', 'I have played golf there before').

rubrics_metrics.name: Past-perfect (pluperfect) tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Formed with had + past participle; denotes an action completed before another past time or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to sequence past events ('by the time we stopped to check the map, the rain had begun falling').

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-perfect tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Formed with will have + past participle; denotes an act expected to be completed before some other future act or time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the entomologist will have collected sixty more specimens before the semester ends', 'the court will have adjourned by five o'clock.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive (continuous) tenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive tenses show continuing or ongoing action and can be formed for present/past/future and their perfect counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active progressive examples: present progressive (he is playing), present-perfect progressive (he has been playing), past progressive (he was playing), past-perfect progressive (he had been playing), future progressive (he will be playing), future-perfect progressive (he will have been playing). Passive progressive: use 'being' + past participle for present/past passive progressive (I am being dealt the cards; I was being dealt the cards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb person
rubrics_metrics.description: Person indicates whether the act/state belongs to first (speaker), second (addressee), or third (other) person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate verb forms to reflect person distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb number and agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: A verb must agree in number (singular/plural) with its subject; only third-person present-indicative singular changes form regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular subject takes singular verb ('the solution works'), plural subject takes plural verb ('the solutions work'). When subjects are joined by 'and' the verb is plural; with 'or'/'nor' the verb agrees with the last-named subject. Collective nouns may take singular or plural verbs depending on unity vs plurality of sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of indefinite pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefinite pronouns (anybody, anyone, everyone, nobody, somebody, etc.) routinely take singular verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'everyone receives credits for this course', 'somebody knows where the car is.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative pronouns as subjects (agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative pronoun used as the subject of a clause is singular or plural depending on its antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tricky construction: 'one of those who/that' — the verb should agree with the antecedent (employees) not 'one' ('She is one of those employees who work tirelessly' is better than '...who works tirelessly'). Reordering the syntax can reveal the agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: False attraction to predicate noun
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject and predicate noun differ in number, the subject governs the verb even if a plural predicate noun might mislead the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid changing the verb to match a following predicate noun; better to rework the sentence if awkward. Examples: Poor: 'My downfall are sweets.' Better: 'My downfall is sweets.' Best: 'Sweets are my downfall.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading connectives (as well as, along with, together with)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrasal connectives that add to a singular subject do not make the subject plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let intervening phrases mislead agreement. Example: Poor: 'The bride as well as her bridesmaids were dressed in mauve.' Better: 'The bride as well as her bridesmaids was dressed in mauve.' Best: 'The bride and her bridesmaids were dressed in mauve.' If singular verb sounds awkward, rephrase with 'and' or restructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement in first and second person and awkward or/either-or constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal pronouns require verb forms that correspond to person; constructions joined by or/either-or/neither-nor traditionally take the verb agreeing with the nearer subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'either he or I am in for a surprise', 'either you or he is right', 'neither you nor I am a plumber'. Because such constructions are awkward, writers often recast them ('one of us is in for a surprise').

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary verbs (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary (helping) verbs are irregular verbs used with other verbs to form voice, tense, and mood; they precede the principal verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common auxiliaries are discussed (modals, do, have, be). See cross-reference 5.103 for more context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal auxiliaries (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modal auxiliaries express ability, necessity, possibility, willingness, obligation, and similar modal meanings; they indicate the principal verb's mood and are often defective (missing some inflected forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider each modal's nuances (can/could, may/might, must, ought, should, will/would) and their appropriate contexts; specific guidance for each follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Can" and "could"
rubrics_metrics.description: Can expresses ability, capacity, or permission (informally); could is the past indicative or a softer future possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can lacks infinitive and participle forms (use 'to be able to'). Use can for ability/permission ('you can carry this trunk'), colloquially for permission ('can I go to the movies?'), and for general possibility ('storms can be severe'). Could denotes past ability ('she could hum a tune at six months') or is a less definite future possibility ('we could travel to Cancun if you wanted to').

rubrics_metrics.name: "May" and "might"
rubrics_metrics.description: May denotes permission or possibility; might often expresses greater doubt or contrary-to-fact hypotheticals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'may' for permission ('you may go') or likelihood ('we may get there on time'); 'might' for stronger doubt or hypothetical contrary-to-fact ('we might have been able to make it'). In negating permission, 'must not' can be stronger than 'may not'.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Must"
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotes necessity arising from will, circumstances, or rule/obligation; also expresses logical conclusion (inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Must' lacks some inflected forms and is used with a bare infinitive: 'we must finish this design', 'all applications must be received by May 31 to be valid'. For obligation or inference use 'must'; in legal contexts prefer 'must' or 'shall' as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Ought"
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotes duty or reasonable expectation and expresses probability or conclusion; more emphatic than should but less than must.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always used with an infinitive ('they ought to fix the fence', 'they ought not to have ignored the signal'). 'To' is sometimes omitted after 'not' in colloquial use, but better usage includes it ('you ought not to worry').

rubrics_metrics.name: "Should"
rubrics_metrics.description: Past-indicative form of shall used for all persons; conveys duty, compulsion, expectation, inference, or speaker attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used with a principal verb: 'they should be at home', 'you should clean the garage today', 'the package should have been delivered today'. 'Should' and 'ought' are often interchangeable; 'should' is slightly less emphatic and more frequent.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Will" and "would"
rubrics_metrics.description: Will expresses future or volition/etc.; would is the past indicative for all persons and expresses conditionals, typical behavior, or past habitual actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'she will be at her desk tomorrow', 'I would recognize the house if I saw it again', 'she would read for hours on end'. 'Will' also conveys certainty, offers, and requests ('will you stop that!').

rubrics_metrics.name: "Do" as auxiliary and principal verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Do functions as a dummy auxiliary for emphasis and question/negation formation and as a principal verb meaning perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Do' has do/does/did and past participle done. As auxiliary: 'we do plan', 'did you speak?', imperatives: 'do not touch!'. As principal verb: 'he does well in school'. 'Do' can substitute to avoid repetition ('Marion dances well, and so do you').

rubrics_metrics.name: "Have" as auxiliary and principal verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Have forms perfect tenses as an auxiliary and denotes obligation/possession/action as a principal verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Have' forms: have/has/had; used with past participle for present/past perfect ('I have looked everywhere', 'he had looked for a better rate'). With an infinitive, 'have' can denote obligation ('I have to finish this paper'); in past obligation 'had to'. As principal verb: possession or experience ('she has a car').

rubrics_metrics.name: "Be" verbs: forms and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Be' has eight forms (be, is, are, was, were, been, being, am) and is used as a principal verb (exist), auxiliary (progressive, perfect), passive marker, and linking verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses: existence ('I am'), auxiliary ('I was born'), progressive ('the train is coming'), passive ('a signal was given'), linking ('truth is beauty'). Also appears in compounds (would-be, has-been). Prefer changing many passive 'be' constructions to active voice where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugation specifics of "be"-verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugation of 'be' differs from other verbs: special present forms (am/is/are), present participle 'being', past forms (was/were), and past participle 'been'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperative is 'be' (e.g., 'be yourself!'). Present participle used with am/is/are for progressive passive ('I am being stalked'). Past indicative uses 'was' for first/third singular and 'were' for others. Past participle 'been' used with perfect forms ('I have been').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs: definition and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs qualify, limit, describe, or modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, or entire clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: modifying verbs ('she studied constantly'), adjectives ('the act was really unusual'), adverbs ('he moved very swiftly'), prepositions ('the birds flew right over the lake'), clauses ('apparently you forgot...'). Some words categorized as adverbs include not, please, the infinitival 'to', and particles in phrasal verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence adverbs modify an entire sentence, often indicating doubt or emphasis of certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'fortunately, we've had rain this week', 'undoubtedly he drove his car to the depot'. Common sentence adverbs include maybe, possibly, however.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbial suffixes (-ly and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many adjectives form adverbs with -ly (or -ally after -ic); spelling adjustments apply for endings like -y, -e, -le, double consonants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spelling notes: happy → happily, shy → shyly; adjectives ending in -e often drop the vowel (true → truly). Avoid awkward -ly adverbs (ghastlily); rephrase or use a phrase ('in a ghastly manner'). Other suffixes: -style, -sideways, -ward, -wise; phrases can take adverbial suffixes ('matter-of-factly'). Not every -ly word is an adverb (lovely is adjective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs without suffixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many common adverbs have no identifying suffix (e.g., almost, never, here, now, just, seldom, late, near, too).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these adverbs and avoid over-normalizing adverb formation when not needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple (flat) versus compound and phrasal adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple adverbs are single words; flat adverbs are bare forms that may work instead of -ly forms. Phrasal adverbs are multiword units; compound adverbs appear as single-word compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat adverbs (drive slow, hold on tight) are common and sometimes preferable in informal imperatives. Some flat adverbs have distinct meanings from -ly forms ('I am working hard' vs 'I am hardly working'). Use compound adverbs sparingly because they can make tone stuffy (notwithstanding, heretofore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbial degrees: positive, comparative, superlative
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs have three degrees: positive (basic), comparative (compare two), and superlative (compare three or more); formation varies by syllable and -ly endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-syllable adverbs not ending in -ly often take -er/-est (sooner, hardest). Multisyllable adverbs usually use more/most or less/least (more ineptly, most acutely). Exceptions exist (early → earlier/earliest). Synthetic vs periphrastic forms exist; irregular adverbs (badly → worse → worst) require dictionary consultation. Many adverbs are noncomparable (never, eternally, now).

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncomparable adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adverbs are absolute by definition and cannot be compared (e.g., eternally, never, uniquely), and many adverbs of time, place, number, or position are noncomparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forming comparative/superlative forms for inherently noncomparable adverbs (e.g., don't say 'more never'). Use contextual rephrasing instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of adverbs (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs should generally be placed as near as possible to the word they modify to avoid ambiguity or miscues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example ambiguity: 'the marathoners submitted their applications to compete immediately'—does immediately modify 'compete' or 'submitted'? Better: 'the marathoners immediately submitted their applications to compete.' Misplaced adverbs can change meaning entirely ('we nearly lost all our camping equipment' vs 'we lost nearly all our camping equipment'). Adverbs express time, place, manner, degree, reason, consequence, and number—place accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs modifying words other than verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: When an adverb qualifies an adjective, another adverb, a preposition, or conjunction, it should immediately precede the word it qualifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'our vacation was very short' (adverb before adjective), 'the flight took too long' (adverb before adjective), 'your fence is partly over the property line' (adverb before preposition), 'leave only when the bell rings' (adverb before conjunction). Group adverbs with the adjective they modify (adjective cluster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs that modify intransitive verbs (placement exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an adverb qualifies an intransitive verb, it generally follows the verb, with some common adverbs preceding the verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally: 'the students sighed gloomily when homework was assigned' (adverb follows verb). Exceptions: always, never, often, generally, rarely, and seldom may precede the verb ('mountaineers seldom succeed in climbing K2'). Place adverbs to reflect intended emphasis and idiomatic usage.
